title: Non-Commutative Cramer's Rule via Quasideterminants
description: Extends Cramer's Rule to division rings using the Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminant. For 2×2 systems Ax = b, the solution x₀ = |A|₀₀⁻¹·(b₀ - a₀₁·a₁₁⁻¹·b₁) is proved correct, unique, and shown to reduce to classical Cramer's Rule when D is commutative.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified over any DivisionRing D.
originalContributions: Defined quasidet₀₀ and quasidet₁₁: Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminants for 2×2 matrices
Defined ncSolve: explicit solution formula for non-commutative 2×2 systems
Proved ncSolve_row0 and ncSolve_row1: correctness of each row equation
Proved nc_cramers_rule: the main theorem Ax = b via mulVec over DivisionRing
Proved nc_kernel_trivial: the kernel is trivial when quasideterminant is invertible
Proved quasidet_mul_eq_det: commutative reduction to classical determinant

sections.title: Quasideterminants
sections.summary: Defines the (0,0) and (1,1) quasideterminants for 2×2 matrices over a division ring. The (0,0)-quasideterminant $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} \cdot a_{10}$ is the Schur complement of the (1,1)-entry.

sections.title: Solution Formula
sections.summary: Defines `ncSolve`: the non-commutative Cramer solution $x_0 = |A|_{00}^{-1} \cdot (b_0 - a_{01} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} \cdot b_1)$ and $x_1 = a_{11}^{-1} \cdot (b_1 - a_{10} \cdot x_0)$.

sections.title: Correctness
sections.summary: Proves row correctness: `ncSolve_row1` uses left cancellation $a_{11} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} = 1$; `ncSolve_row0` factors out the quasideterminant and cancels $q \cdot q^{-1} = 1$.

sections.title: Main Theorem
sections.summary: **nc_cramers_rule**: proves $A \cdot \text{ncSolve}(A, b) = b$ over any division ring $D$ via `mulVec` with componentwise verification.

sections.title: Uniqueness
sections.summary: Proves kernel triviality (`nc_kernel_trivial`) and solution uniqueness (`nc_cramers_unique`): if $|A|_{00} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 0$, the solution is unique.

sections.title: Commutative Reduction
sections.summary: Shows `quasidet_mul_eq_det`: over a field, $|A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} = \det(A)$, recovering classical Cramer's Rule.

overview.historicalContext: Gabriel Cramer published his rule in 1750 for solving $n \times n$ linear systems via ratios of determinants, but the formula implicitly requires commutativity of the underlying ring. The question of extending determinantal methods to non-commutative settings was taken up by Dieudonné (1943), who defined a determinant over division rings via the Abelianization, and later by Gelfand and Retakh (1991, 1997), who introduced the theory of quasideterminants. For an $n \times n$ matrix, there are $n^2$ quasideterminants (one per entry), each defined as the Schur complement of the complementary $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ submatrix. These quasideterminants satisfy non-commutative analogues of row expansion, heredity, and Sylvester's identity. This formalization proves the $2 \times 2$ case, which is the foundation for the inductive theory.
overview.problemStatement: Can Cramer's Rule extend to non-commutative settings using quasideterminants?
overview.text: For 2×2 systems Ax = b over a division ring D, the quasideterminant |A|₀₀ = a₀₀ - a₀₁·a₁₁⁻¹·a₁₀ provides an explicit solution formula.
overview.proofStrategy: Define the solution via Gaussian elimination (back-substitution from row 2, then use quasideterminant for row 1). Prove correctness by verifying each row equation using left cancellation (a·a⁻¹ = 1). Prove uniqueness via kernel triviality (q·x = 0, q ≠ 0 ⟹ x = 0 in a division ring).
keyInsights: The quasideterminant $|A|_{00} = a_{00} - a_{01} \cdot a_{11}^{-1} \cdot a_{10}$ is exactly the Schur complement of the $(1,1)$-entry, connecting linear system solving to block matrix inversion
Non-commutativity forces careful tracking of multiplication order: $a \cdot b^{-1} \cdot c \neq a \cdot c \cdot b^{-1}$ in general, so left-vs-right cancellation is a proof concern throughout

The solution formula uses left multiplication by inverses ($|A|_{00}^{-1} \cdot (\ldots)$), matching the row structure $Ax = b$ where $A$ acts on the left; a right-action formulation $xA = b$ would require right quasideterminants
Over a commutative field, $|A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} = \det(A)$, so the quasideterminant solution reduces to the classical $x_i = \det(A_i) / \det(A)$ formula

Uniqueness follows from kernel triviality: the Gaussian-elimination proof that $|A|_{00} \cdot x_0 = 0$ forces $x_0 = 0$ in a division ring (no zero divisors), a property that fails over general non-commutative rings
prerequisites: Schur complements and block matrix theory

conclusion.summary: Cramer's Rule fully extends to $2 \times 2$ systems over division rings via quasideterminants. The formalization proves correctness ($A \cdot x = b$), uniqueness (kernel triviality), and commutative reduction ($|A|_{00} \cdot a_{11} = \det(A)$) with 0 sorries and 0 axioms -- a fully verified result.
conclusion.implications: This validates the Gelfand-Retakh quasideterminant framework as the correct non-commutative analogue of determinants. The kernel triviality argument demonstrates that division rings (no zero divisors) are the natural setting for unique solvability. The $2 \times 2$ case is the inductive base for the general $n \times n$ quasideterminant theory, where the $(i,j)$-quasideterminant is defined by Schur-complementing the $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ submatrix obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$.
openQuestions: Can this be generalized to $n \times n$ matrices using the full quasideterminant theory and its heredity identities?
What is the precise relationship between quasideterminants and the Dieudonné determinant (which maps to the Abelianization $D^*/[D^*, D^*]$)?
Can the quasideterminant framework be formalized for matrices over more general non-commutative rings (e.g., Ore domains)?
